checks.note: Seen in the post: multi-agent (Opus 4 lead, Sonnet 4 subagents) beat single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2% on the internal research eval. Agents use about 4x the tokens of chat and multi-agent systems about 15x. On BrowseComp three factors explain 95% of performance variance and token usage alone explains 80%; the other two are the number of tool calls and model choice. Upgrading to Sonnet 4 gave a larger gain than doubling the token budget on Sonnet 3.7. The eval started from about 20 queries. Correction: the 80% is variance in BrowseComp performance across runs. It is not a measured split of the 90.2% gap between multi-agent and single-agent, so 'token spend explained most of the quality difference' stretches what the post says.
checks.corrected_claim: Anthropic reports that its multi-agent system beat single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2% on an internal research eval, at about 15x the tokens of chat. Separately, on BrowseComp, token usage alone explained 80% of the variance in performance, and with tool-call count and model choice 95%.
checks.corrected_number: 90.2%; about 4x (agents vs chat) and 15x (multi-agent vs chat); 80% / 95% of variance on BrowseComp; Sonnet 4 upgrade beat doubling the Sonnet 3.7 budget
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: A vendor engineering post that is not peer reviewed and that no one independent has repeated. The internal eval started from about 20 queries and was judged by an LLM. The post gives no matched-token single-agent baseline. The variance analysis is on BrowseComp, not on the internal eval. Models: the Claude 4 generation.

checks.note: Seen in the post: effort rules of 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls for simple fact-finding, 2-4 subagents for direct comparisons and more than 10 for complex research. The lead spawns 3-5 subagents in parallel and subagents use 3+ tools in parallel, which cut research time by up to 90% on complex queries. An early failure was spawning 50 subagents for simple queries. Because context beyond 200,000 tokens is truncated, the lead saves its plan to memory. Subagents run synchronously, which the post names as a bottleneck. Domains that need shared context are a poor fit, and most coding has fewer parallel subtasks. The '10-15 calls each' for comparisons is from the reader; the fetch confirmed only '2-4 subagents', so treat the per-subagent call count as unverified by me.
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: One vendor's research system, self-reported. The width rules have no ablation and no numbers behind them. The 90% time cut applies to complex queries. No independent replication.

checks.note: Table 5 in the HTML (current version) matches: turns 7.2 / 11.4 / 26.1 / 27.7 / 44.3 (overhead 58% / 263% / 285% / 515%); success per 1K tokens 67.7 / 42.4 / 23.9 / 21.5 / 13.6; trace-level error amplification 17.2 independent, 7.8 decentralized, 5.1 hybrid, 4.4 centralized, 1.0 single. I saw the turn exponent myself: T = 2.72 x (n + 0.5)^1.724, R2 = 0.974. Mean reasoning budget is 4,800 tokens per trial. The current version reports 260 configurations; I did not check v1's 180. The paper also gives task-level error amplification of only about 1.1-1.3, much smaller than the trace-level figures.
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: A preprint by Google-affiliated and academic authors, not yet independently replicated. 1 to 4 agents, six benchmarks, three model families (OpenAI, Google, Anthropic). The turn-exponent fit uses architecture-aggregated means. The error amplification quoted is trace-level; the task-level figure is about 1.1-1.3.

checks.note: Finance-Agent single-agent baseline 0.349: centralized +80.8%, decentralized +74.5%, hybrid +73.1%. PlanCraft baseline 0.568: centralized -50.3%, decentralized -41.5%, hybrid -39.1%, independent -70.0%. The interaction coefficient is -0.236 (p = 0.004), with a threshold of about 45% single-agent accuracy. The tool-coordination term is -0.096 (p = 0.002). Cross-validated R2 is 0.373 to 0.413. All seen in the HTML.
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: Same study as L2-03: one preprint, not replicated, at most 4 agents. The predictive model explains only about 40% of the variance. The 45% threshold is a fitted value, and each conclusion rests on two benchmarks.

checks.note: Seen in the HTML. Table 2 (Gemini-2.0-Flash): HumanEval 90.2 to 93.2, MBPP 79.6 to 80.8, GSM8K 93.8 to 94.6; the original ChatGPT-based gains were +10.7, +16.0 and +9. Table 3: prefill 1.20x to 220.22x (GSM8K 34.66x) and decode 2.10x to 21.64x; the paper's prose gives narrower ranges than its own table. Table 4 cascade: GSM8K 94.8% at 1,056 normalized tokens vs multi-agent 93.6% at 8,837; AIME 38.3% at 64,879 vs 81,159. About 80% of examples are ties. Appendix B.4 says the cascade only works if results can be checked easily and accurately (exact match). The abstract says 'up to 20%' cost reduction and the introduction says 88.1%; the 88.1% does not appear in the tables. Affiliation is UIUC. Scope is 15 datasets, 7 tasks and 9 frameworks.
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: A single academic preprint, not replicated. Mostly Gemini-2.0-Flash. Cost is measured in normalized tokens. The cascade assumes a cheap, exact checker. The cost-saving figures are inconsistent across sections.

checks.note: Table 1 averages at 1,000 thinking tokens: single 0.418, sequential 0.379, debate 0.388, parallel-roles 0.381, subtask-parallel 0.369, ensemble 0.333 (a single-agent variant SAS-L scored 0.397). Benchmarks are FRAMES and MuSiQue 4-hop. Models are Qwen3-30B-A3B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B, Gemini-2.5-Flash and Gemini-2.5-Pro. Budgets run from 100 to 10,000 thinking tokens. Affiliation is Stanford. In the degradation test, sequential multi-agent overtook single only under heavy masking or substitution (Qwen3, MuSiQue). The authors flag the Gemini budget-control artifact. The paper is inconsistent on whether the judge is a separate model or the same model.
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: One preprint (April 2026), not replicated. Multi-hop QA with no tools. Only thinking tokens are matched. The degradation result comes from one model on one benchmark, and the judge is ambiguous.

checks.note: Seen in the HTML. Replacing the Orchestrator with a GroupChat orchestrator (no ledgers, planning or loop detection) dropped GAIA validation performance by 31%. Removing a single agent cost 21% (Coder, Executor/ComputerTerminal) to 39% (FileSurfer). The stall threshold was at most 2, and worker contexts are reset after each plan update. The progress ledger asks five questions. The most frequent error codes were persistent inefficient actions and insufficient verification steps. On WebArena, Magentic-One with GPT-4o scored 32.8% against Jace.AI's 57.1%. On the GAIA test set it scored 32.33% (GPT-4o), and on AssistantBench 25.3% accuracy.
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: Microsoft Research, GPT-4o, 2024. The ablation is on the GAIA validation subset only and changes ledgers, planning and loop detection together. No independent replication of the ablation.

checks.note: Seen in the post: with locking, twenty agents ran at the effective throughput of two or three, and locks were held when agents failed or forgot to release them. Planners can spawn sub-planners, workers do not coordinate with each other, and a judge decides whether to continue, after which the next cycle starts fresh. The integrator role was removed because it created more bottlenecks than it solved. The authors call the system 'nowhere near optimal' and say periodic fresh starts are still needed against drift. They preferred GPT-5.2 for planning and long runs. No throughput numbers are given for the final design. Corrections: the post says the agents ran for close to a week and wrote over 1 million lines across about 1,000 files; it does not say a browser was completed in a week. The post gives no number showing that the hierarchy 'fixed most of' the problem.
checks.corrected_claim: Cursor reports that coordinating peer agents through locks made twenty agents run at the throughput of two or three. A planner/worker/judge hierarchy with fresh cycles worked better, but the post gives no throughput figure for it.
checks.corrected_number: 20 agents at the throughput of 2-3 under locking; the browser run took close to a week and wrote more than 1M lines across about 1,000 files; no throughput number for the final design
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: A self-reported vendor blog with no controlled comparison and no independent replication. Long-running coding only. The outcome depends on the model (GPT-5.2 was preferred over Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1-Codex).

checks.note: The abstract says success is on average 30% lower when working together than when one agent performs both tasks (the Solo setting). The benchmark has over 600 tasks (652 feature pairs), 12 repositories and 4 languages (Python, TypeScript, Go, Rust). The three failure causes match. The affiliations listed are Stanford University and SAP Labs US. The body reports that GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 4.5 reach about 25% in the Coop setting, roughly 50% below Solo.
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: One benchmark paper, not replicated. Two agents edit shared repositories concurrently. The paper's internal counts of features and task sets differ between sections.

checks.note: Seen in the post by Walden Yan (2026-04-22). Multi-agent works best when one agent writes and the others add judgment. Managers were overly prescriptive, assumed they shared state with child agents, and children did not report back by default. A small primary model (SWE-1.5) could not tell when it was at its limits. Devin Review averages 2 bugs per PR, roughly 58% severe; note this is on PRs written by Devin. The post gives no cost numbers for the multi-agent patterns.
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: Practitioner opinion plus the vendor's own product data, with no controlled test. The bug figure applies to Devin-written PRs and is marketing-adjacent.

checks.note: Read through the ar5iv HTML; the arXiv PDF fetch was unreadable. Table 6 (Appendix G.2, 20 documents): GPT-3.5-Turbo 75.8% at index 0 and 53.8% at index 9, below its 56.1% closed-book score (Table 1). Claude-1.3 ranges from 60.1% (last position) down to 55.9% (index 4), a gap of 4.2. LongChat-13B goes from 68.6% to 52.5%, a gap of 16.1. The gaps are best versus worst position; for Claude the best position is the end, not the start. The 'worse than closed-book' result holds clearly for GPT-3.5-Turbo; Claude and LongChat stay above their closed-book scores.
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: 2023-era models on multi-document QA and key-value retrieval only. Below-closed-book performance is shown for GPT-3.5-Turbo, not for every model. Current models may differ.

checks.note: Chroma technical report (July 2025): 18 models across Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Qwen. LongMemEval used 306 prompts, about 113k tokens full versus about 300 focused, and every family scored significantly higher on the focused form; Claude showed the largest gap, mostly from abstentions. One distractor lowered scores and four lowered them more. Shuffled haystacks scored better than coherent ones. The text gives no single headline accuracy percentage.
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: A vendor technical report (Chroma sells retrieval), not peer reviewed and not independently replicated. Synthetic tasks and LongMemEval only. Not every model ran every experiment.

checks.note: Seen in the HTML (JetBrains Research and TU Munich). Qwen3-Coder 480B: raw 53.4% at $1.29, masking 54.8% at $0.61, summary 53.8% at $0.64. Summary runs were about 15% longer than raw and 13% longer than masking. Gemini 2.5 Flash took 52 turns with summary versus 44 with masking. Gemini 2.5 Flash with thinking: raw 40.4%, masking 36.4%, summary 31.4%. The limits were 250 turns, SWE-bench Verified with 500 instances, and five model settings; the OpenHands window went from M=10 to a tuned 58. Corrections: masking savings range from 9.8% to 57.1% (about 51-57% if the Qwen3-32B thinking outlier is excluded). Summary calls cost 0.65% to 7.20% of the total, not 3% to 7%. The hybrid result (7% cheaper than masking, 11% cheaper than summary) comes from the 50-instance Verified-50 subset. Under thinking, masking also lost solve rate (36.4%), not only summary.
checks.corrected_claim: Masking roughly halved cost and matched summarization on solve rate in most settings. With Gemini 2.5 Flash thinking, both methods lost solve rate against raw context. The hybrid's extra savings were measured on a 50-instance subset.
checks.corrected_number: Masking 9.8%-57.1% cheaper than raw; summary calls 0.65%-7.20% of cost; summary runs about 13-15% longer; hybrid 7% / 11% cheaper on Verified-50; thinking setting raw 40.4%, masking 36.4%, summary 31.4%
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: One preprint on SWE-agent and SWE-bench Verified with five model settings. Window sizes are tuned to the scaffold. Coding tasks only, not orchestration. No independent replication.

checks.note: The abstract matches the numbers: compactors kept 17% of injected side constraints on average; an agent deleted emails without approval in 30 of 100 post-compaction sessions versus none before; a separate constraint extractor reached over 90% retention in all three scenarios. Corrections: the arXiv title is 'Lost in Context Compaction: When LLM Systems Drop Side Constraints', and there are five authors (Zhiqi Wang, Yichi Zhang, Dongwon Lee, Nathalie Baracaldo, Yuchen Yang), not two. The evaluation suite is called CONPACT. The abstract does not name the models or compactors.
checks.corrected_claim: In the CONPACT suite, the compactors tested kept only 17% of side constraints on average; 30 of 100 inbox sessions deleted emails without approval after compaction versus 0 before; storing constraints separately gave over 90% retention.
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: One preprint (2026), with only the abstract read. Models and compactors are unnamed. Retention varied with the compactor, context length, phrasing and position. Not replicated.

checks.note: Overall scores were Factory 3.70, Anthropic 3.44 and OpenAI 3.35, judged by GPT-5.2. Artifact trail scores were 2.45, 2.33 and 2.19, giving the 2.19-2.45 range. Compression ratios ran from 98.6% to 99.3%. The dataset is 36,611 messages (methodology section) and there are four probe types. Factory's method is 'anchored iterative summarization', which merges only the newly truncated span. The separate artifact index is offered as a suggestion, not tested.
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: Run by the vendor whose method won, with an LLM judge. Production coding sessions only, not peer reviewed and not independently replicated.

checks.note: The abstract matches: for GPT-5.5 completion went from 80% to 85% (p = 1.0) while retrieval calls rose from 21.0 to 63.9 (p = .002). Retrieval rose in all six model-regime comparisons, and five of six stayed significant after Holm correction. Irrelevant retained content raised retrieval by 57% (p < .001). There was no retrieval surge in ALFWorld. The setup used a 24-turn limit, three models and two regimes. The completion figures are at the prespecified 5x compression; DeepSeek's completion fell only at 10x.
checks.conditions_that_limit_it: A single-author preprint (August 2026), with only the abstract read. One deterministic planning environment, and the effect did not appear in ALFWorld. Three models. Not replicated.
